Chapter 8: The Logic of Orthodoxy—Sanity in a Mad World.
You know, when the world feels upside down, finding some real, solid sanity can seem almost impossible. People are always chasing after the next big idea, hoping they've finally unlocked the secret to happiness. But so often, all that chasing just leaves us more confused than before.
What if I told you, the old faith—with all its paradoxes—actually gave us a kind of sanity? It offered a way of seeing the world that helped everything make sense, even the contradictions.
Imagine this: a group of friends, each with their own doubts and opinions, sitting around and talking about the meaning of life. Their conversation goes in circles. Everyone stands their ground, defending their own perspective. But then, someone suggests, “Hey, what if we look at the old stories—the creeds and confessions that shaped generations before us?”
The whole mood changes. Arguments fade, and instead, people start listening. They wonder—could there be a wisdom deeper than our own opinions?
See, the old faith never ran from questions. In fact, it welcomed doubt. But it also offered answers—answers that had survived the toughest tests of time.
It taught that the world is both broken and beautiful. That people are both fallen and beloved. That truth can be mysterious, and yet still knowable.
Most of us don’t realize just how much we need this kind of sanity. The world today is so full of noise and confusion, it’s easy to lose your grip on what’s actually real. But the old faith gave us a way of seeing that was both humble and confident—a way to live that made room for reason, but also for wonder.
And here’s something powerful: orthodoxy isn’t about escaping reality. It’s about engaging with it even more deeply. It’s having the conviction that the world does make sense, that truth is real, and that the greatest adventure of all is to seek it with an open heart.
